states.name: California
timeline: Matei Zaharia, a PhD student in Berkeley's RAD Lab, begins Spark to run on the Mesos cluster manager
Spark's code is released as open source in early 2010: about 3,900 lines of Scala
Berkeley launches the AMPLab (Algorithms, Machines and People), which carries Spark forward
The RDD paper wins the best paper award at NSDI in San Jose (April)
Seven Berkeley researchers behind Spark found Databricks; Andreessen Horowitz leads a $14 million first round
The first Spark Summit draws more than 450 people to San Francisco (2 December)
A Databricks team sorts 100 terabytes in 23 minutes on 206 cloud machines, a shared world record
Google launches Cloud Dataproc, managed Spark and Hadoop, in beta (September)
The AMPLab closes after six years (December); the RISELab follows in 2017
Databricks open-sources Delta Lake, a transactional table layer for Spark (April)
Databricks donates its pipeline framework to Spark as Declarative Pipelines (June)

events.title: Spark begins
events.text: Matei Zaharia, a PhD student in Berkeley's RAD Lab, starts Spark for jobs that reuse the same data again and again.

events.title: Built on Mesos
events.text: Spark is first written to run on Mesos, a Berkeley cluster manager begun as a class project in spring 2009.

events.title: Open-sourced
events.text: Spark's code is released as open source in early 2010: about 3,900 lines of Scala.

events.title: Working sets
events.text: At HotCloud in Boston (June), the first Spark paper reports jobs up to 10x faster than Hadoop on iterative machine learning.

events.title: AMPLab opens
events.text: Berkeley's Algorithms, Machines and People Lab launches in early 2011 and carries Spark forward.

events.title: $10 million grant
events.text: On 29 March, at a White House big-data event, the NSF announces a five-year Expeditions grant to the AMPLab.

events.title: The RDD paper
events.text: "Resilient Distributed Datasets" wins the best paper award at NSDI in San Jose (April).

events.title: Shark
events.text: Shark, which ran SQL queries on Spark, is presented at SIGMOD in New York (June).

events.title: Into Apache
events.text: Spark is accepted into the Apache Incubator on 21 June.

events.title: Databricks founded
events.text: Seven Berkeley researchers behind Spark found Databricks; Andreessen Horowitz leads a $14 million first round.

events.title: Spark Streaming
events.text: "Discretized Streams" is presented at SOSP in Pennsylvania (November): streams as a series of small batches.

events.title: First Spark Summit
events.text: More than 450 people from 13 countries meet in San Francisco on 2 December.

events.title: Top-level project
events.text: On 27 February Spark becomes a top-level Apache project, with code from more than 120 developers.

events.title: Spark 1.0
events.text: Spark 1.0 is released on 30 May, with Spark SQL included as an alpha.

events.title: Sort record
events.text: Spark sorts 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 machines, tying a UC San Diego team; Hadoop's record took 72 minutes on 2,100.

events.title: DataFrames
events.text: Spark 1.3 (13 March) adds DataFrames: tables with named columns, in Python, Scala and Java.

events.title: Catalyst
events.text: The Spark SQL paper describes Catalyst, the optimiser that rewrites DataFrame and SQL plans.

events.title: Spark on EMR
events.text: Amazon makes Spark a standard option on its Elastic MapReduce cloud service (June).

events.title: IBM's commitment
events.text: IBM calls Spark the most important new open-source project in a decade and puts 3,500 people on it (June).

events.title: Cloud Dataproc
events.text: Google launches Cloud Dataproc, managed Spark and Hadoop clusters, in beta (September).

events.title: Spark 2.0
events.text: Spark 2.0 (26 July) unifies DataFrames and Datasets and ships Structured Streaming as an experiment.

events.title: AMPLab closes
events.text: The AMPLab ends in December after six years; the RISELab takes its place in 2017.

events.title: Streaming ready
events.text: Spark 2.2 (11 July) removes the experimental label from Structured Streaming.

events.title: AWS Glue
events.text: AWS Glue, which runs Spark jobs without servers to manage, becomes available on 14 August.

events.title: Azure Databricks
events.text: Microsoft's Azure Databricks becomes generally available on 22 March.

events.title: Streams as tables
events.text: The Structured Streaming paper is presented at SIGMOD in Houston (June).

events.title: Delta Lake
events.text: Databricks open-sources Delta Lake, ACID tables on cloud storage for Spark, on 24 April.

events.title: Spark 3.0
events.text: Spark 3.0 (18 June) adds adaptive query execution; Python is now Spark's most used language.

events.title: Adaptive by default
events.text: Spark 3.2 (13 October) turns adaptive query execution on by default.

events.title: Spark Connect
events.text: Spark 3.4 (13 April) adds Spark Connect, a thin client that talks to a remote Spark cluster.

events.title: Microsoft Fabric
events.text: Microsoft Fabric, with Spark for data engineering, becomes generally available in November.

events.title: Spark 4.0
events.text: Spark 4.0 (23 May): over 5,100 tickets from more than 390 contributors; ANSI SQL by default.

events.title: Declarative Pipelines
events.text: On 11 June Databricks donates its pipeline framework to Spark as Declarative Pipelines.

events.title: Snowpark Connect
events.text: Snowflake starts running Spark DataFrame code on its own engine, with no Spark cluster (2025).

events.title: Real-time mode
events.text: Spark 4.1 (16 December) adds a real-time mode for millisecond-latency streaming.

events.title: ACM Prize
events.text: Matei Zaharia, now a Berkeley professor, receives the ACM Prize in Computing (April).

events.title: Spark 4.2
events.text: Spark 4.2.0 (14 July): over 1,700 tickets from more than 250 contributors, with geospatial types.

chartNote: Share of the area of the contiguous United States, by the kind of the most recent landmark of Spark's story in each present-day state: a simplification, since California had every kind at once and Spark runs in data centres everywhere. Large states such as Texas and Montana swing the shares. The Apache Software Foundation, a worldwide community, is placed at its registered address in Delaware; work outside the US is not shown.
